In Germany and while traveling around Europe, I often had this small fear in the back of my mind.

Don’t leave your bag on the café table.
Watch your pockets.
Be careful walking down a dark street.
Check if someone is standing too close.
It was normal to be cautious.

But after moving to Korea, my feeling of safety changed a lot.
Suddenly, I saw people leaving laptops, bags, and phones unattended in cafés. Not because they were careless, but because this is how many people save their seat before ordering.

For Germans, it felt almost like putting a towel on a beach chair.

I remember being at a festival in Seoul. I left my picnic blanket with my wallet, phone, and camera on it. After spending hours near the stage, I came back and everything was still there.

Walking around Korea, even late at night, often feels calm. Streets are bright, there are people around, and CCTV is everywhere. In Germany, many people value privacy and are more critical of surveillance. In Korea, many people seem to feel safer because of it.
There is also less fear of being mugged or pickpocketed.

Of course, this does not mean nothing ever happens. Umbrellas and bicycles are a different story, and roads can feel dangerous. Cars do not always respect zebra crossings, delivery bikes can pass too close, and buses sometimes feel like roller coasters.

So no, Korea is not perfect.

But the big difference for me is peace of mind.

Losing something also feels different here. Many times, you can retrace your steps and find it again. Cafés may even post forgotten items on Instagram so the owner can recognize them. There is also a lost and found system that adds another layer of comfort.

It was not only about low crime.
It was about not having to be constantly on guard.
News headlines can make South Korea look tense from the outside. But daily life here can feel very different from what people imagine.

Sometimes you need to experience a country firsthand to understand what safety really feels like.

And for many foreigners living in Korea, that peace of mind is one of the biggest reasons they choose to stay.

posts.title: The CLARITY Act stalled. The compliance burden did not.
posts.author: Ben dhaya Ahmed

The CLARITY Act stalled. The compliance burden did not.

The US Senate voted 49–50 on the procedural motion to advance the country’s most significant crypto market structure bill. It needed 60 votes.

For founders, exchanges and investors, this is not simply a political setback. It means key questions remain unresolved:

• Where does SEC authority end and CFTC authority begin?
• When can DeFi developers be held responsible for how their code is used?
• How should stablecoin rewards and yield be treated?
• What legal protection can businesses rely on while the framework remains unsettled?

Crypto businesses cannot pause their operations until Congress reaches agreement.

In practice, regulatory uncertainty shifts more responsibility onto product design, legal opinions, contracts, listing due diligence and documented risk decisions.

A legal opinion is not permanent protection. Its value depends on its jurisdiction, scope, assumptions, reliance terms and whether it is reviewed when the rules change.

At Infinilex, our work begins where the headlines end: helping Web3 teams translate regulatory uncertainty into clear decisions, documented risk positions and jurisdiction-specific readiness.

If your US market entry, token launch, exchange listing or DeFi product depends on the CLARITY Act passing, now is the time to stress-test the legal foundation rather than wait for certainty.

posts.title: Yesterday, the US Senate voted on the most important crypto bill in history.
posts.author: Elena Ageyonok
posts.snippet:
Yesterday, the US Senate voted on the most important crypto bill in history.

49 said yes.
50 said no.

The room went quiet.

"This one stings," said Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse.
"It's over," said Sen. Lummis - the bill's biggest champion - before the final tally was even in.
(Source: The Block, CoinDesk, September 15, 2026)

I've been thinking about this since last night.
Not about the vote. About what the industry actually spent to get here.

Years. Hundreds of millions of dollars. The most coordinated political campaign crypto has ever run in Washington. Exchanges, executives, lobbyists, former regulators - all pulling in the same direction for the first time.

And what did they get?

Agency guidance. The same rules they already had. Rules that the next administration can reverse on day one without a single congressional vote.

Michael Saylor had a characteristically sharp take after the vote: "The only clarity you need is Bitcoin."

He was being glib. But there's something true in it.

Bitcoin has had regulatory clarity in the US for years. It's a commodity. Full stop. No ambiguity, no jurisdictional fight, no Senate drama.

Everything else - every token, every protocol, every exchange - is still navigating a framework designed for a world that existed before blockchain was invented.

And here's the part that nobody is saying clearly enough:

This bill didn't die because of anything crypto did wrong.

It died because of a fight over whether sitting presidents should be allowed to profit from assets they're simultaneously regulating. The crypto industry got caught in a battle that was never really about crypto at all. It was about Trump's $1.4 billion in digital asset holdings - and whether Washington could agree on what to do about that.

The answer, apparently, is no.

Four Republicans crossed the aisle to vote against their own party's bill. Democrats held firm. The coalition that passed it 294-134 in the House simply doesn't exist in the Senate.

So now what?

Midterms are in seven weeks. Both chambers are heading home to campaign. The next Congress seats in January - under whatever political configuration November produces.

For every compliance officer sitting down to build their 2027 regulatory budget right now - the answer is the same as it was yesterday, and the year before that.

More uncertainty. More legal opinions. More waiting.

That's the real cost of 49-50.

Does this get resolved in 2027 - or does uncertainty just become the permanent US regulatory posture for crypto? 👇
posts.reason: Thoughtful analysis of CLARITY Act failure and regulatory uncertainty for crypto businesses is directly relevant to founders facing unresolved legal frameworks.

comments.text: The point that gets lost is that agency guidance was never going to disappear just because the bill did - it just means the SEC and CFTC keep deciding jurisdiction through enforcement rather than through a text Congress agreed on, which is a much slower and more expensive way to get clarity.

If the coalition that passed the House bill doesn't exist in the Senate, is there any real appetite left to decouple market structure reform from the conflict-of-interest fight, or are they now permanently tied together?

We went through the MiCA transitional period on the EU side, and even with a finished text, VASPs are still discovering that 'clarity' on paper does not mean a smooth CASP authorisation file - the US is now facing that same gap without even having the text.

Thoughts on the AI Threat
  
  
          An active debate has sprung, questioning whether AI leaders are attempting to ring fence their own dominance, create legal firewalls to isolate from liability. The President has weighed in.
  
          The intrusions of technology come on you so slowly you hardly realize they’re happening. I try to isolate myself as much as possible…but you really can’t avoid it, can you?
  
          New AI efforts to get me to give access to my accounts. You know, it steps into my vendor and performs analysis. I would be assured, that all the safeguards are in place to protect the use. I am also sure that people don’t know what they don’t know. And so, assurances can never be complete.
  
          To me, the real threat posed by AI is that the risk will come from the usual cast of bad actors. Can we believe, for a second, that they are not bending all oars in the water to use AI to level up the playing field? Why spend decades trying to prepare to fight the US Navy  when you might be able to cripple the power grid from a keyboard?
  
          Why mess around trying to hack a crypto wallet when your efforts might be more profitable going for the major leagues of finance?
  
          You might think I’m giving bad people bad ideas, but any belief that they haven’t thought of this already would be naïve. Not only have they, but I would bet they are trying, every day, every moment. 
  
          And then when one gazes into the near future and attempts to game the emergence of quantum computing, running AI on that technology, you can’t be anything but sobered up. 
  
          There is nothing written in the laws of the universe that intelligence has to be biologically sourced. There is nothing that says bad intent has to reside in flesh and blood.           If an AI model is smart enough to analyze my portfolio, what do I do if it wants a piece of it? Don’t snicker…look at the adventures people get in crypto wallets.
  
          This may sound like someone caught in the backdraft of the future, you know, unable to get with the program and so, being left behind in all the change.
  
          Quite the opposite, I’m afraid. I know who Kurzweil and Heisenberg were.

posts.title: WHEN £5 MILLION BECOMES THE SHADOW BEHIND £72 MILLION
posts.author: KEMI ATANDA ILORI
posts.snippet:
WHEN £5 MILLION BECOMES THE SHADOW BEHIND £72 MILLION

Political controversies rarely remain in separate boxes.

They accumulate.

That is Nigel Farage’s difficulty.

The £72 million donated to Reform UK by Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne did not arrive on politically virgin territory.

Farage is already the subject of a Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards investigation concerning an alleged failure to register an interest involving a £5 million personal gift from Harborne.

Farage disputes wrongdoing and has described the earlier arrangement as private.

That distinction matters.

An investigation is not a conviction.

An allegation is not proof.

But politics has another courtroom:

public opinion.

And the optics are difficult.

A billionaire associated with a multimillion-pound personal gift to a politician subsequently gives £36 million to that politician’s party.

The legal questions are for the proper authorities.

The political question writes itself:

Where does personal benefaction end and political patronage begin?

Then add another ingredient.

The Metropolitan Police is investigating allegations concerning possible breaches of foreign-funding rules after an undercover investigation into Reform figures. Reform denies wrongdoing.

Again: investigation is not guilt.

But political narratives do not wait patiently for all investigations to conclude.

They accumulate nouns:

Millions.

Donors.

Police.

Parliament.

Foreign funding.

Crypto billionaires.

And eventually the nouns become a sentence in voters’ minds.

That may be deeply unfair.

It may ultimately prove groundless.

But political parties ignore perception at their peril.

Reform’s danger is no longer simply whether individual allegations are substantiated.

It is whether voters begin joining the dots before investigators do.

Because in politics, sometimes the story arrives at the polling station long before the verdict.

posts.title: Product language does not decide regulatory classification.
posts.author: Cryptoverse Legal - Crypto Lawyers in Dubai
posts.snippet:
Product language does not decide regulatory classification.

Advisory Services: Recommendations or opinions concerning virtual assets, particularly where presented as suitable for a customer.

Management and Investment Services: Discretionary or managed deployment of customer virtual assets under an agreed mandate.

Lending and Borrowing Services: Arrangements through which virtual assets are lent, borrowed, collateralised or deployed to generate a return.

Derivatives Services: Futures, options, perpetuals and other products deriving value from virtual assets or creating leveraged exposure.

A “wallet” may legally function as a lending product. “Copy trading” may involve advice, management or both. A leveraged token can create derivatives exposure despite being purchased through a spot interface.

Launching a crypto investment or yield product? Obtain a classification opinion before designing the customer journey.

posts.title: Dubai's biggest developers may be quietly building fintech arms of their own. 🏗️➡️💠
posts.author: CA Nandagopi Nalajala
posts.snippet:
Dubai's biggest developers may be quietly building fintech arms of their own. 🏗️➡️💠

A small line in Binghatti Holding's H1 2026 financials caught my attention: among its newly incorporated subsidiaries is Advanced Virtual Assets L.L.C. — 100% owned, incorporated in 2026, principal activity listed as "Virtual Assets Broker & Dealer Services."

And this is a group reporting real scale:
 📈 Revenue: AED 9.5bn
 📈 Net profit: AED 3.0bn
 🏗️ Revenue backlog: AED 17.3bn

Put it next to what DAMAC has already done — a DAMAC-built apartment was the first property tokenised on Dubai Land Department's PRYPCO Mint platform, and DAMAC Group signed a ~$1bn deal with MANTRA to tokenise real-world assets — and a pattern starts to form:

Large developers may increasingly want to own the digital-asset infrastructure around their real estate, not just leave it to crypto-native firms.
And the government is putting a number on it: DLD projects tokenised real estate could reach AED 60bn (~$16bn) — about 7% of Dubai's total property transactions — by 2033, under the Dubai Real Estate Sector Strategy 2033.
And this opens a new revenue rail for developers and platforms, not just the regulator. If tokenised volumes approach that AED 60bn target, even the low fees typical of these platforms could plausibly translate into high hundreds of millions of AED per year in fee income — a genuine recurring-revenue stream, on top of the rental income that flows to token-holders. (Illustrative only — actual figures depend on volumes, turnover and fee mix.)
Early platforms are also working hard to pull retail investors in — with low entry points (from ~AED 2,000) and early incentives to encourage first-time participation.

Why it could matter:
 🔹 Fractional / tokenised ownership can widen the investor base
 🔹 New capital channels could complement bank debt and Sukuk
 🔹 A new fee-based revenue line for developers and platforms
 🔹 Secondary-market infrastructure could improve liquidity for tokenised assets

That said, the space is still early, and results so far have been mixed — some tokenisation ventures and their partners have seen real volatility and uneven traction. So this isn't really a technology story. The real test will be licensing, custody, investor protection, governance — and, most of all, actual liquidity.
Is this the start of a genuine real estate–fintech convergence in Dubai, or will virtual-asset infrastructure stay a niche for a few large players?

I write about real estate finance, IFRS 15 and capital structuring in the UAE — always open to connecting with others working at the intersection of property and finance.

Sources: Binghatti Holding H1 2026 financial statements; Dubai Land Department & VARA announcements; publicly reported company news. Views are my own.

Circle just launched Arc mainnet.

An open Layer 1 built for financial markets and agentic activity, going live with native USDC, 100+ applications, and validators including BlackRock, Mastercard, and Visa.

Here's what caught my attention today 👇

1️⃣ Noah: CLARITY or Not, America's Status as the World's Crypto Hub Is Not in Doubt 🇺🇸

2️⃣ dLocal: Why Stablecoins Are Becoming a Payments Infrastructure Shift 🌎

4️⃣ Mastercard and Bank of Khyber (BoK) Partner to Accelerate Digital Payments 🇵🇰

6️⃣ Circle Launches Arc Mainnet, an Economic Operating System for the Internet 🇺🇸

The shift?

Circle is no longer content issuing the stablecoin, it wants to own the chain it runs on. Launching Arc as a purpose-built Layer 1 for finance, with BlackRock, Mastercard, and Visa as validators, is a bid to become the base layer for onchain money itself, not just a token that lives on someone else's network. If the biggest names in traditional finance are validating your chain, the line between crypto infrastructure and financial infrastructure has effectively disappeared.

Which do you think is the bigger prize in stablecoins: issuing the dominant token like USDC, or owning the settlement layer everything runs on like Arc?

posts.title: One more crypto exchange is shutting down this year, and the reason reveals a troubling reality about the economics of running an exchange.
posts.author: Nitin Gupta
posts.snippet:
One more crypto exchange is shutting down this year, and the reason reveals a troubling reality about the economics of running an exchange.

CoinEx Global announced on September 15 that it will wind down after 9 years, with operations ending on December 22.

The exchange says reserves remain above 100%, has published proof of reserves, and is giving users roughly three months to withdraw. Remaining CET will be bought back at its original $0.005 listing price.

I’ve been watching crypto infrastructure closely, and CoinEx is not alone. BitMEX, BitMart, AscendEX, and CoinEx have all announced shutdowns or orderly wind-downs in 2026.

The economics are getting harder for mid-sized exchanges.

CoinEx ranked around 33rd by trading volume, with roughly $58 million in daily volume against $174 million in assets.

More importantly, TRM Labs traced more than $3.84 billion in flows between CoinEx and sanctioned Iranian entities.

That makes founder haipo yang’s comment particularly relevant... “Carrying unlimited risk for limited revenue is no longer a rational choice.”

The pressure is structural. 

Trading volume concentrates around deeper-liquidity venues. Compliance costs remain significant regardless of scale. And a single sanctions, security, or fraud issue can create liabilities far beyond the revenue generated by a customer.

That gap isn't market conditions. It's whether customer assets were actually there all along. A wind-down is simply when everyone finds out.

I think crypto is consolidating into a handful of deep-liquidity venues plus specialised regional players with real licences. The middle disappears.

The surviving advantage stops being token listings, it becomes provable solvency, clean flows, and jurisdictions you can actually operate in.

If your exchange closed tomorrow, would you get your money back?

Building an AI agent is easier than it looks. You can use Claude or ChatGPT and talk to them in plain English.

Most people only see the surface. They use natural language and think that is enough. This works for general tasks. It fails for specific, professional use cases.

To build a custom agent, you must understand the machinery behind the curtain. I built a Crypto Research Assistant. It answers questions using specific data sources. Even this small project taught me four massive lessons.

1. The Agent Loop
An agent rarely gives an answer in one step. It calls tools, gets results, and feeds those results back into the model. It repeats this until it has the right information.

2. The RAG Pipeline
You need a way to handle data. This involves four steps:
- Chunking
- Embedding
- Retrieval
- Generation
The agent uses this pipeline as a tool to find answers.

3. Evaluations (Evals)
How do you know if the answer is correct? You must test for two things:
- Leak: Does the agent guess from its memory instead of your data?
- Over-refusal: Does the agent refuse to answer when it actually knows the truth?

4. Deployment
You cannot just upload your private documents to the cloud. I used a specific stack:
- GitHub for code.
- S3 buckets for document storage.
- Streamlit for the user interface.

Three hard lessons I learned the long way:

Stop chasing 100% accuracy.
LLM responses change every time. You cannot fix every prompt error perfectly. Pick one target, improve it, and move on. Do not fall into a trap of endless tweaking.

Watch your token usage.
Testing your system costs money and tokens. Set a usage cap. Give the agent the latest response for context so it does not rerun everything from scratch.

Avoid over-optimized chunking.
I built a chunker that worked for one article but failed for multiple documents. If a chunk is too long, you hit token limits. If it is too short, the model loses context. Build for variety, not just one specific file.

If you want to build agents for specific business needs, you must understand these layers. Otherwise, you will never get the results you want.

posts.title: 600W + <25 km/h - could this make low-speed E2Ws more useful in India?
posts.author: Shivam C.
posts.snippet:
600W + <25 km/h - could this make low-speed E2Ws more useful in India?
Having been in the EV industry for a while, I’ve often wondered whether more power at low speed could make these vehicles more practical for real-world Indian conditions - carrying a pillion, climbing flyovers, handling gradients or supporting last-mile delivery.

MoRTH’s draft G.S.R. 760(E) proposes a 30-minute motor power of <0.6 kW (600W) while retaining a maximum speed of <25 km/h. It also specifies suitable brakes, front and rear retro-reflectors, certification by a Rule 126 testing agency and compliance with AIS-049 safety requirements. The existing 60 kg criterion is also proposed to be removed.

More power, but still outside the motor-vehicle definition - while adding formal certification and safety requirements.

- The opportunity: more practical low-speed mobility, potentially lower cost of ownership and greater scope for last-mile applications.
- The question: as power and vehicle capability increase, should safety, testing and enforcement evolve accordingly?

Markets such as #China and #Vietnam show how widely electric 2Ws can be adopted, although their vehicle categories and regulatory frameworks are different.

So perhaps the debate isn't simply 250W vs 600W.
It is about finding the right balance between utility, affordability, safety and regulation.

Could a more capable low-speed E2W category become an important part of India’s next phase of electric mobility?

posts.title: The biggest threat to AI competition may be the people trying to save us from it.
posts.author: Uno Alexander Veski, MBA
posts.snippet:
The biggest threat to AI competition may be the people trying to save us from it.

The irony is extraordinary.  We could end up with the government protecting consumers from AI by protecting the largest AI companies from their competitors.

That is not competition. That is a cartel wearing a safety helmet.

The proper question is not:  “How do we stop AI from moving too fast?”

It is: “How do we make the people who cause identifiable harm bear the cost without making innovation itself a privilege reserved for incumbents?”

Competition is not the enemy of safety. Competition is the mechanism by which better, cheaper and safer technologies emerge.

There is an old economic lesson that applies perfectly to AI: When an industry discovers that government can protect it from competition, it has an incentive to spend more time lobbying than innovating.

The language is always noble: safety, standards, responsibility, the public interest.
But follow the incentives. If compliance costs billions, the largest laboratories can afford them. A startup cannot.

If only a handful of companies can satisfy the regulatory requirements, those companies acquire something more valuable than a technological moat: a government-created moat. That is how regulation can become the opposite of what it claims to be.

Regulate harmful conduct. Be extremely cautious about regulating the development of the technology itself.

If an AI company commits fraud, violates privacy, causes demonstrable consumer harm, or deploys a dangerous system irresponsibly, punish the conduct.

But telling companies how fast they may innovate is a different proposition. It is the economic equivalent of putting a speed limit on every automobile because some drivers crash. 

And there is an even more dangerous possibility: letting the largest AI companies coordinate to slow the frontier.

That may be proposed in the language of safety. But economically, competitors agreeing to restrict competition is precisely the sort of arrangement antitrust law exists to scrutinize. OpenAI has already sought clarity about whether coordinated frontier slowdowns could violate antitrust law.

And the moment government becomes the gatekeeper of who is permitted to build the future, we should stop asking only what the regulation protects us from.
We should ask: Who does the regulation protect from competition?
posts.reason: Thoughtful analysis of AI regulation and compliance costs creating barriers to competition; directly relevant to deep tech founders facing EU AI Act requirements.

comments.text: The AI Act already builds in a version of this tension - its risk-tiering was meant to scale obligations to actual risk, but the compliance burden on general-purpose model providers is still substantial enough that it favours incumbents with in-house legal and technical capacity to demonstrate conformity.
Where do you draw the line between regulating conduct after the fact and requiring ex ante conformity assessments, given that the AI Act already commits to the latter for high-risk systems?

We advise deep tech founders on AI Act readiness, and the recurring issue isn't the substance of the obligations but the documentation burden - that's precisely where a well-resourced incumbent has an advantage a startup doesn't.

posts.title: 📜This one is for leaders ⚖️
posts.author: Karthick Thoppe

📜This one is for leaders ⚖️

The rapid adoption of generative AI has dramatically accelerated engineering and R&D cycles across Europe. However, this massive leap in productivity has introduced a critical dilemma regarding intellectual property and attribution: when an AI system co-creates enterprise-grade code, pharmaceutical compounds, or complex architectures, determining legal ownership becomes dangerously complex. 

In this article I explore the legal, ethical, and regulatory realities of AI-assisted innovation in the European market.

* With the transparency obligations of the EU AI Act (Article 50) officially in effect as of August 2026, managing AI output is no longer just an internal policy issue... it is a strict regulatory requirement. 

* European Patent Office (EPO) and EU copyright laws firmly restrict IP ownership and inventorship to human beings. Tech leaders, CTOs, and legal teams must understand these frameworks immediately. 

* Failing to properly document human conception or comply with new AI Act mandates risks invalidating highly valuable IP portfolios, alienating top engineering talent, and triggering massive regulatory fines of up to €15,000,000 or 3% of global turnover.

Read on for my views on establishing an actionable playbook... that is simply a four step strategy for updating engineering workflows, contracts, and internal culture to protect your organisation's assets. 5 mins reading time.

comments.text: Worth noting Article 50 is a transparency obligation, not an ownership rule - it does not touch inventorship or authorship at all. The IP exposure comes separately from the EPO's and CJEU's insistence on a human contributor, which means the real fix is documenting the human's conceptual contribution at each stage, not just labelling AI-generated output.

On the four-step playbook, does it address how to evidence 'sufficient human contribution' where the AI output is only lightly edited before filing - that threshold is where most of the disputes we see actually sit.

We are increasingly asked to review patent and copyright files after the fact where nobody kept a record of who did what during AI-assisted development, and reconstructing that trail retroactively is far harder than building it in from day one.

posts.title: LA ERA DE LA INMEDIATEZ: CUANDO UNA SOCIEDAD PREMIA LA ESTUPIDEZ

posts.snippet:
LA ERA DE LA INMEDIATEZ: CUANDO UNA SOCIEDAD PREMIA LA ESTUPIDEZ

El periodo actual se encuentra marcado por una paradoja difícil de ignorar: nunca habíamos tenido un acceso tan amplio al conocimiento y, simultáneamente, tantos incentivos económicos para producir contenido intelectualmente irrelevante.

En México, 86.1% de las personas de seis años o más utilizó internet durante 2025. La economía de la atención convirtió ese acceso en un mercado donde un influencer puede obtener ingresos extraordinarios bailando en paños menores, exhibiendo riqueza, vendiendo productos de pésima calidad o prometiendo dinero fácil, mientras investigadores, ingenieros, médicos, profesores y científicos dedican décadas a su formación sin recibir una fracción comparable de atención o recompensa económica.

El problema no es que alguien baile frente a una cámara y gane dinero; comienza cuando una sociedad confunde VISIBILIDAD con MÉRITO, POPULARIDAD con CONOCIMIENTO y RIQUEZA con INTELIGENCIA.
China parece haber comprendido parcialmente este problema. Durante 2025, el Ministerio de Ciencia y Tecnología impulsó la promoción pública de científicos e investigadores mediante exposiciones, conferencias y reconocimientos. En 2026, espacios publicitarios y pantallas que tradicionalmente exhibían productos y celebridades comenzaron a mostrar científicos como Qian Xuesen, Yuan Longping, Tu Youyou y Deng Jiaxian.
El mensaje cultural es poderoso: una sociedad también decide quiénes son sus celebridades.

China también ha endurecido la regulación del contenido profesional en internet, incluyendo la verificación de determinadas credenciales para contenidos especializados y nuevas obligaciones sobre marketing financiero digital.

Occidente debería estudiar seriamente este fenómeno.
Una civilización no se construye mediante videos de quince segundos. Semiconductores, medicamentos, sistemas financieros, satélites, infraestructura y modelos matemáticos existen porque generaciones dedicaron años a resolver problemas difíciles que probablemente nunca se volverían virales.

La estupidez individual puede ser inocua. Convertida en fenómeno colectivo y acompañada de ignorancia, corrupción y abuso de poder, puede deteriorar instituciones, productividad y educación durante generaciones.
Una guerra destruye vidas e infraestructura de manera inmediata y visible; la degradación educativa e institucional puede destruir el futuro de una sociedad silenciosamente durante décadas, como en mi hermoso México.

Una sociedad revela sus prioridades no solamente mediante aquello que enseña, sino mediante aquello que ADMIRA.

¿A quién estamos convirtiendo nosotros en celebridad? ¿Prostitutas virtuales, vendehumos, estafadores y defraudadores?

#Educación #Ciencia #Tecnología #Investigación #México #China #Sociedad

Parquets sintéticos. Suelos vinílicos con ftalatos. 
 El riesgo químico oculto en tu hogar

El peor material para hacer tierra en casa

¿Sabías que tu suelo vinílico podría estar liberando disruptores endocrinos en tu casa durante años? 🏠⚠️

Los suelos vinílicos (PVC/SPC) son muy populares por su precio y facilidad de instalación. Pero hay un problema grave: muchos contienen FTALATOS, químicos que la Agencia Europea de Sustancias Químicas (ECHA) clasifica como disruptores endocrinos.

¿QUÉ SON LOS FTALATOS?

Son compuestos químicos que se añaden al PVC para darle flexibilidad y resistencia. El problema es que no están químicamente unidos al plástico, por lo que se liberan constantemente al ambiente durante 5-10 años.

RIESGOS PARA LA SALUD:
🔴 Disrupción hormonal: Alteran el sistema endocrino.
Problemas de fertilidad: Afectan a la reproducción.

🟡 Desarrollo fetal: Riesgo durante el embarazo
Alteraciones neurológicas: Especialmente en niños.

🔵 Alergias y asma: Irritación respiratoria

LA REALIDAD:
Estás respirando e ingiriendo estos químicos constantemente al tenerlos en tu hogar. Es como tener un "producto químico activo" liberándose 24/7 en tu espacio vital.

LA SOLUCIÓN:

✅ Busca suelos SIN FTALATOS (Phthalate-Free).

✅ Marcas como Meister ofrecen vinílicos sin ftalatos.

✅ Pregunta siempre por la composición química. 

✅ Considera alternativas naturales: corcho, madera maciza con aceites naturales, barro cocido.

CONCLUSIÓN:
No todos los suelos vinílicos son iguales. Exige transparencia y elige productos que no comprometan tu salud a largo plazo.

posts.title: 🚨 ¿Puede una demanda dirigirse contra una sociedad que todavía no era, formalmente, la sucesora de la entidad que había celebrado el contrato?
posts.author: Iván Mateo Borge
posts.snippet:
🚨 ¿Puede una demanda dirigirse contra una sociedad que todavía no era, formalmente, la sucesora de la entidad que había celebrado el contrato?
El TS acaba de matizar una regla procesal fundamental: la "perpetuatio legitimationis" no puede aplicarse de forma automática cuando las circunstancias del caso hacen que su aplicación estricta conduzca a un resultado puramente formalista. La STS (Sala 1.ª) núm. 1034/2026, de 25 de junio, aborda esta cuestión en un litigio sobre una cláusula suelo.
🔹 ANTECEDENTES: Los demandantes ejercitaron en 2017 una acción declarativa de nulidad de una cláusula suelo y reclamación de cantidades frente a Banco Santander, en relación con un préstamo hipotecario inicialmente concedido por Banco de Andalucía.
El problema: en el momento de presentarse la demanda, Banco Popular —que había absorbido previamente a Banco de Andalucía— todavía no había sido absorbido jurídicamente por Banco Santander. La fusión por absorción no se protocolizó hasta septiembre de 2018, inscribiéndose posteriormente. Banco Santander alegó, por ello, falta de legitimación pasiva: cuando se presentó la demanda, todavía eran dos sociedades jurídicamente diferenciadas.
🔹 ¿QUÉ DICE EL TS? El Alto Tribunal desestima el argumento.
Es cierto que la regla general derivada de la litispendencia es que la legitimación se determina atendiendo a la situación existente al interponerse la demanda (art. 410 LEC), por lo que la decisión del tribunal debe referirse a la situación de hecho y de derecho existente en ese momento. Pero esa regla no es absoluta. En este caso concurrían circunstancias singulares; a saber:
 ✅ El Banco Santander ya era titular del 100 % de las acciones de Banco Popular antes de la demanda.
 ✅ La demanda identificaba expresamente la conexión sucesoria entre ambas entidades.
 ✅ La posterior fusión supuso una sucesión universal de la relación jurídica litigiosa.
 ✅ Y, además, Santander pudo defenderse plenamente durante el procedimiento.
Por ello, aplicar mecánicamente la "perpetuatio legitimationis" habría conducido a un planteamiento estrictamente formal y a un resultado «artificioso y dilatorio», contrario a la buena fe procesal.
⚖️  DOCTRINA CLAVE: La "perpetuatio legitimationis" constituye la regla general, pero puede modularse cuando las circunstancias concretas del caso lo exijan. La finalidad de las reglas procesales no puede quedar desplazada por un formalismo que, en un supuesto de sucesión universal, no aporta una verdadera garantía y únicamente conduce a reiniciar o duplicar actuaciones. En definitiva  👉 La legitimación procesal no puede analizarse al margen de la realidad jurídica y económica del litigio.
Una sentencia especialmente interesante para los supuestos de fusiones, absorciones y sucesión procesal, donde el momento exacto en que se produce la sucesión puede convertirse en una cuestión procesal decisiva. Tenlo en cuenta  👇  👇  👇

posts.snippet:
Estos días tuve la oportunidad de participar de Dreamforce 2026 en San Francisco, representando a ueno bank S.A. , itti y Grupo Vázquez SAE junto a Ursula Krochik , Melina Andrea Di Rosa y Juan Ignacio Olivares  

Más allá de los lanzamientos, me llevo varias ideas interesantes después de escuchar a Marc Benioff , CEO de Salesforce; Dario Amodei , CEO de Anthropic; Sam Altman, CEO de OpenAI; Jensen Huang , CEO de NVIDIA; y Omar Sultan AlOlama , Ministro de Estado de Inteligencia Artificial de Emiratos Árabes Unidos.

Algunos aprendizajes que me quedaron:

• La interfaz empieza a dejar de ser el producto. Con Aiforce, Salesforce plantea un modelo donde su plataforma, sus datos y sus procesos pueden vivir detrás de distintas interfaces como Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini o Slack. La UI empieza a construirse de manera mucho más dinámica alrededor de cada usuario y cada contexto.

• El desafío pasa de incorporar IA a integrarla con el negocio real. Los modelos probabilísticos necesitan convivir con procesos, permisos, datos y reglas determinísticas para poder operar dentro de una empresa.

• Los agentes empiezan a desafiar la ciberseguridad. Sam Altman habló de cómo agentes cada vez más capaces obligan a repensar los modelos tradicionales de seguridad, especialmente a partir de los incidentes recientes con sistemas autónomos (Huggingface)

• En ventas, el contexto en tiempo real pasa a ser parte central del CRM. Capturar actividad mientras sucede, detectar oportunidades en riesgo, resumir automáticamente el trabajo de los equipos y utilizar agentes para encontrar nuevos leads cambia bastante la lógica tradicional de carga y seguimiento comercial.

• En servicio, no alcanza con automatizar conversaciones. El foco empieza a estar en agentes que resuelven, aprenden de cada interacción y ayudan a optimizar continuamente los canales de atención.

• Y probablemente el aprendizaje que más me quedó fue de Omar Sultan Al Olama: la adopción de IA no es solamente un problema tecnológico. Es también un problema de educación, confianza, regulación y acceso.

Su planteo sobre acercar a quienes innovan con quienes regulan me pareció especialmente relevante. También la decisión de Emiratos de capacitar masivamente a su población y a empleados públicos en IA para que la transformación tecnológica no deje a las personas sin herramientas para adaptarse.

Una frase que resume bastante de lo que me llevo de Dreamforce: la discusión ya no parece ser si vamos a trabajar con agentes de IA, sino cómo construimos empresas e instituciones preparadas para hacerlo de manera útil, segura y responsable.

posts.title: Who is my MP? It is one of the most searched questions about UK politics, and the answer has always been sitting in Parliament's own open data. This year I built two free iOS apps
posts.author: Philip Brumpton
posts.snippet:
Who is my MP? It is one of the most searched questions about UK politics, and the answer has always been sitting in Parliament's own open data. This year I built two free iOS apps on top of it: Who Is My MP?, which finds your MP by postcode, and The Lords, which helps you find members of the House of Lords by their specialist interests.

Why build a UK Parliament app now?

Fifteen years ago I was Lead Designer at Dod's Parliamentary Communications, a departure from the ecommerce and advertising work I was used to. Instead of optimising CTR and conversion, the material was MPs, peers, select committees and the machinery of Westminster.

This year I went back to that world on my own terms. Everything Parliament publishes about both Houses (votes, speeches, written questions, registered interests, committee memberships) is free through Hansard and the Parliament data services. The data has been there for years. What is thin on the ground is a well designed way in for ordinary people.

Not a gotcha app

The easy version of an MP app is a gotcha: expenses, attendance leagues, who turned up least. I did not want to build that.

I wanted to show what MPs actually do, presented without editorial framing, and to be honest about the limits of the data. An MP with a low number of sitting days might also be a practising doctor, and the raw number tells you nothing about that. So the apps present the parliamentary record and let people read it in context, rather than ranking anyone. Neutral and non-partisan, with no spin.

How do I find out who my MP is?

Enter your postcode into Who Is My MP? and the app finds your MP and constituency. From there you get a full profile built entirely from Parliament's own data:

how your MP has voted in the Commons
what they have said in debates, straight from Hansard
the written questions they have tabled
their registered interests
the select committees they sit on
the roles they hold and their election results

Everything links back to the source on parliament.uk. It is written in SwiftUI with no third party packages, talking directly to the Parliament Members, Votes, Hansard and Written Questions APIs, with postcodes.io handling the postcode lookup.

Is there an app for the House of Lords?

The second app needed a very different approach. Nobody has "their" peer. The Lords is not organised by geography, so a postcode is no use. What peers do have is deep specialist knowledge: medicine, transport, the law, the arts, defence, the Windrush generation, palliative care.

So The Lords is browse-first. Instead of a search box and a blank screen, you start from topics and professions. Searching "end of life care" or "railways" maps onto the categories Parliament uses behind the scenes, so you find peers with a registered interest or professional background in that area, along with their voting record and register of interests.

It is the app you open when you think "who in the Lords actually knows about this?"

What the UK Parliament APIs taught me

The data is excellent and the documentation is patchy, a familiar combination. A few things I learnt the hard way:

The Commons votes API silently caps results at 25 per request, so pagination is not optional.
Constituency names need normalising before search (ampersands, "and", punctuation) or you get nothing back.
In rural areas a postcode can sit a long way from where someone is standing, so location lookups need a widening fallback.
Hansard search and Hansard overview endpoints use different parameter conventions for the same fields.

Both apps are free on the App Store now.

Who Is My MP? find your MP by postcode: https://whoismymp.uk
The Lords, find peers by interest: https://thelords.app

If you work in politics, journalism, policy or civic tech, I would like to hear what you make of them, and what you would want a UK Parliament app to do next.

posts.title: States agree on elements for a future treaty on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems
posts.author: Mateus Kowalski
posts.snippet:
States agree on elements for a future treaty on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems

In recent weeks we have been flooded with doomsday warnings about AI, including predictions of human extinction within a generation. Politicians, researchers and even some of the major tech companies have been calling for AI governance and regulation.

Against that backdrop, there is a signal of hope. After several years of negotiations, the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (GGE LAWS) has adopted by consensus its final report, which sets out normative elements that could form the basis of a future treaty.

At 3:00 am on Saturday, 5 September, in a room of an otherwise dark and empty Palais des Nations in Geneva, exhausted delegates celebrated the conclusion of the work. We felt it as an historic moment: a light switched on in the dark.
Among other points, states agreed on:

– the requirement of human control and judgment across the weapon's entire life cycle;
– a list of measures needed to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law (IHL);
– the understanding that responsibility always lies with states, parties to armed conflict and humans, never with machines.
(See paras. 25–44 of the final report, linked below.)

The result is not perfect. The negotiations did not aim to develop new law. Instead, they produced a coherent set of elements understood as the corollary of applying existing international law, and IHL in particular, to LAWS. Still, states with very different perspectives and interests on these weapons managed to bridge their differences and find common ground. That is significant, all the more so in the current geopolitical climate.

Treaty negotiations are unlikely to begin any time soon. But these elements now serve as a benchmark for states’ conduct in developing and using LAWS, and for their failure to act.

Going forward, it will be interesting to see how those outside the room interpret the agreed elements: academia, tech companies, the defence sector, combatants. Many of the elements carry subtle nuances. They reflect a delicate balance reached after tough negotiations, which may not be easy to grasp for those who were not part of the process. In the end, it all comes down to human judgment.

For now, a step in the right direction.

LAWS is not only the acronym for these weapons systems. Laws are also the norms and principles that ensure AI is governed for the common good of humanity, rather than becoming a doomsday technology.

🔗 Final report [https://lnkd.in/e2npAT6t]

#LAWS #AutonomousWeapons #IHL #AIGovernance #CCW

comments.text: The framing that responsibility always sits with states and humans, never machines, matters more than it looks - it forecloses the accountability-gap argument that has been used to slow down regulation of autonomous systems generally, not just weapons.

📈 THE AI BOOM HAS CREATED A NEW QUESTION FOR SHARIAH-CONSCIOUS INVESTORS: WHICH AI STOCKS ACTUALLY PASS THE SCREEN?

AI is becoming one of the most important investment themes in global markets.

But for Shariah-conscious investors, technological growth is only one part of the equation.

A company can be at the centre of the AI revolution and still require careful screening of its business activities, debt, cash/securities and non-permissible income.

🟢 EXAMPLES CURRENTLY PASSING AAOIFI-BASED SCREENS

Recent halal.sh screening data lists companies including:

• NVIDIA (NVDA)
• Alphabet (GOOG)
• TSMC (TSM)
• Samsung Electronics
• Micron Technology (MU)
• Arm Holdings (ARM)

For example, halal.sh's current AI-stock screen lists NVIDIA, TSMC, Samsung, Micron and Arm among companies passing its AAOIFI-based methodology.

NVIDIA's latest screen, updated against its July 2026 filing, reports debt of 0.66% of market capitalisation, cash/securities of 1.96%, and interest income of 0.73% of revenue, all within the stated screening thresholds.

🔴 BUT SOME MAJOR TECH NAMES CAN FAIL

Microsoft (MSFT) is an interesting example.

Its balance-sheet ratios pass the cited thresholds, but halal.sh's August 2026 analysis reports 7.55% prohibited income versus a 5% threshold, resulting in a non-compliant classification under that methodology.

This illustrates an important point:

A STRONG BALANCE SHEET DOESN'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN SHARIAH COMPLIANCE.

🧮 WHAT DOES THE SCREEN LOOK AT?

AAOIFI-based equity screening can involve:

Business activity → Debt → Cash/securities → Non-permissible income

The exact methodology and interpretation matter, which is why investors should examine the underlying screening standard rather than rely on a simple “halal” label.

And there is another distinction worth remembering:

Shariah compliance ≠ comprehensive ethical screening.

A company may pass financial Shariah ratios while investors may separately consider questions around defence, geopolitics, environmental impact or customer use of its technology.

💡 THE BIGGER INVESTMENT LESSON

The AI revolution isn't just creating new technology.

It is creating new questions about how capital should participate in technological growth.

For Shariah-conscious investors, the process therefore isn't simply:

“Is AI growing?”

It is:

“Does this company fit my financial, Shariah and broader ethical criteria?”

And because financial statements, market capitalisation and business activities change, screening should be treated as an ongoing process—not a permanent label.

From Belgium to Argentina: CJNG’s 52-Kilo MDMA Shipment Seized at Zárate Port
 
A suspected member of Mexico’s Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) was arrested at Argentina’s Zárate port while attempting to recover 52 kilograms of MDMA shipped from Belgium—enough to produce roughly one million ecstasy tablets. posts.title: Stablecoins are being pulled into mainstream tax rules 🪙
posts.author: Amit Rawat AFA MIPA
posts.snippet:
Stablecoins are being pulled into mainstream tax rules 🪙

From 6 April 2027, HMRC will start treating "eligible stablecoins" more like money than crypto for individuals and trustees — and that's a real shift in how digital asset returns get taxed.

Here's what's changing:

• Capital Gains Tax exemption — disposals of eligible stablecoins will no longer trigger CGT for individuals and trustees
• Income Tax instead — interest-like returns on eligible stablecoins will be taxed as savings income under Income Tax, not as a capital gain
• Different rules for companies — corporation tax treatment kicks in from 1 April 2027, with eligible stablecoins treated as a money debt
• "Eligible" has a specific meaning — a stablecoin must maintain a stable value against a fiat currency, backed by fiat or other assets held to support that peg
• A one-off reset — anyone holding eligible stablecoins right before commencement is treated as making a notional disposal and reacquisition at market value, with any gain/loss landing on 6 April 2027
• Legislative footing — the changes were confirmed 13 July 2026 following a Call for Evidence (26 March – 7 May 2026) and will be written into the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 via Finance Bill 2026-27

The direction of travel is clear: HMRC is drawing a line between stablecoins (treated as money-like) and other cryptoassets (still under the standard CGT regime). For anyone holding or building on stablecoins, this changes the compliance picture significantly.

posts.title: The FCA published its final cryptoasset perimeter guidance on 16 September 2026 and stated in the same document that it does not reflect a statutory instrument already laid before
posts.author: thedenouement
posts.snippet:
The FCA published its final cryptoasset perimeter guidance on 16 September 2026 and stated in the same document that it does not reflect a statutory instrument already laid before Parliament. Firms must use it to decide what to apply for when the authorisation gateway opens on 30 September.

THE DEVELOPMENT: PS26/18 makes PERG 18 and amends PERG 1, 2 and 8, following CP26/13 (15 April to 3 June 2026) and 78 responses, 60% broadly supportive. It covers the seven new regulated cryptoasset activities commencing on 25 October 2027, from stablecoin issuance to arranging staking.

The FCA declines the substantive requests: “PERG cannot be used to expand, narrow or otherwise alter the scope of the perimeter established in legislation.” The guidance rests on the Cryptoasset Regulations as passed on 4 February 2026 and “does not yet include the new SI”. A further consultation follows in early Q4 2026, with final amended guidance in early 2027.

BUSINESS MODEL IMPACT: 63% of respondents were unsupportive of the arranging deals guidance, 59% saying it took too broad a view of the activity and too narrow a view of the exclusions. The FCA says the breadth belongs to Parliament, and the technical services exclusion from arranging arrives only with the SI; it has not yet been written into PERG. What does not change: the perimeter was fixed on 4 February 2026, and this document moves none of it, and MLR obligations run concurrently rather than being displaced by FSMA authorisation.

PRODUCT IMPACT: Safeguarding turns on “the requisite degree of control”, and the FCA declined to resolve how that applies to multi-party computation, key sharding and distributed custody, which 55% of respondents on that topic sought. Products using hybrid stabilisation are not qualifying stablecoins. Liquid staking tokens are unlikely to be “solely a record”, so they remain inside the qualifying cryptoasset definition.

REVENUE IMPACT: Nothing moves this quarter. This is guidance rather than rules, and no cost benefit analysis was required. The cost is the authorisation programme, and the date that bites is 28 February 2027, when the window closes for firms relying on the savings provisions.

ACTIONS

The pre-application support service is open to book, and the FCA directs staking applicants to it for the models PERG leaves open.

The Q4 2026 consultation reopens arranging, dealing and UK qualifying stablecoins—the three areas that drew the heaviest objection—so a CP26/13 response that was not taken up has a second hearing coming.

TIMELINE

16 Sep 2026 — PS26/18 published, PERG 18 made
30 Sep 2026 — Authorisation gateway opens
28 Feb 2027 — Window closes for the savings provisions
Early 2027 — Final amended guidance, not yet dated against that cut-off
25 Oct 2027 — Regulated cryptoasset activities commence

Source: https://lnkd.in/ercH4eDH 

#CryptoRegulation #DigitalAssets #FCA #CASP #FinancialRegulation

Proper contracts, invoices and payment records are essential for recovering outstanding amounts.

Protect your business name, brand and other intellectual property where appropriate.

Keep contracts, invoices, receipts and important communications properly documented.

Software development is setting the pace. Vehicle validation has to keep up.
Shorter development cycles and more frequent software releases require sufficient regression testing in every iteration. Yet engineering teams often face a difficult trade-off: fast regression testing can limit coverage, while more comprehensive and realistic testing can slow down the development process and increase reliance on physical prototypes.
For power electronics, meaningful validation also requires realistic voltage and power conditions to adequately capture relevant electrical interactions. At the same time, testing must remain fast enough to fit within agile software development cycles.
AVL Copper Car TS™ brings these requirements together in a system-level validation approach. Real vehicle architecture is combined with precise emulation to extend regression test coverage while maintaining the speed and repeatability needed for software-driven development.

Some of you went silent at the moment that mattered. If that was you, maybe this one's for you.
You started our diagnostic last year. You answered honestly, some of you at length. Then the form asked for an email address and you paused. Some of you never came back. We watched it happen in the data, in real time, in a survey about why organisations go quiet. The silence had turned up inside the instrument built to measure it.

So we rebuilt the survey halfway through. The paper grew a page it didn't know it needed. Somewhere around the fourth midnight, Brenton Webber and I stopped saying "one more week" and started saying nothing at all. Which, given the subject matter, was at least on brand.

It's done. 😮‍💨  The Good CX and Half Time Orange Ltd research is called 'The Silence of the System': 

123 senior leaders across New Zealand and Australia, with 140 total internationally. 
👇
82% of you gather customer feedback. 23% have a clear process to act on it. The gap between those numbers is the paper. The pause at the email field is on page six.

We will be telling you a lot more in the coming weeks
